planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Bride is a selection of the native species Heuchera villosa and is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than most Heuchera cultivars, making it one of the best-performing coral bells for the deep shade and muggy summers of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate summer drought and heavy shade far better than most Heuchera hybrids. Autumn Bride is a selection of Heuchera villosa, the heat- and humidity-adapted native alumroot of the southern Appalachians and Gulf South uplands, chosen for its large, softly fuzzy, chartreuse-green leaves and — most notably — its late bloom time. While most coral bells flower in late spring, Autumn Bride sends up tall, airy, 18–24 inch spikes of small creamy-white flowers in late summer and early fall, right when few other shade perennials are blooming, making it a valuable late nectar source for native bees. Its species-level heat and humidity tolerance make it dramatically more reliable in deep, humid Gulf South shade than the many showy-leaved Heuchera hybrids that decline in southern summers. Excellent massed as a shade groundcover or woodland-edge border plant in zone 4–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Mount Cuba Center — Heuchera Research Trials

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Looking Glass needs consistent moisture and appreciates a spot sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch its thin silver leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered through summer heat and divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring or fall. Looking Glass is a striking Brunnera macrophylla cultivar bred for nearly solid, luminous silver foliage, with only the finest tracery of green veins remaining visible — among the most reflective, brightest foliage of any shade perennial, capable of lighting up a dim woodland bed from a distance. In early spring, sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the emerging leaves before the silver coloration fully develops. The heart-shaped leaves hold their color and quality through the growing season better than many older silver-leaf brunnera cultivars, provided the plant is kept out of hot, direct sun and never allowed to dry out. An outstanding textural and color contrast plant for shaded borders and woodland gardens in zone 3–8.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Bottle Rocket needs steady soil moisture and wilts dramatically in dry spells, though it recovers with watering — best sited at a pond edge, streamside, or damp low spot.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind; mulch to conserve soil moisture and water deeply during dry spells. Bottle Rocket is a compact selection of Ligularia stenocephala, grown for its bold, deeply toothed, dark green leaves and, in mid-to-late summer, dense, upright, narrow spikes of bright yellow flowers that resemble small exploding fireworks or rockets — considerably more compact and garden-friendly than the species and older ligularia cultivars, which can sprawl to 4–5 feet. The strong vertical flower spikes provide valuable late-summer color and form in the shade garden, and the foliage itself is architecturally bold enough to serve as a textural anchor even before bloom. Best used at the moist margins of a shaded water feature, rain garden, or low spot where soil never fully dries out, in zone 4–8.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Spring Symphony forms a slow, well-behaved clump and spreads gently by short stolons, making it suitable for smaller shaded beds and edging.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch with leaf litter or shredded bark to keep roots cool and moist through summer. Spring Symphony is a foamflower cultivar prized for its finely cut, deeply lobed, almost fern-like leaves with a distinct central dark red-brown blotch that intensifies in cooler weather, providing months of foliage interest before and after the bloom period. In mid-spring, slender spikes densely packed with small, star-shaped flowers in soft pink emerge just above the foliage, creating a frothy, foamy display that gives the genus its common name. Its compact, restrained spreading habit makes it easier to keep within bounds than many stoloniferous native Tiarella cordifolia selections, while still knitting together into an attractive, weed-suppressing shade groundcover over a few seasons. Zone 4–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Mount Cuba Center — Tiarella Research Trials

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Pink Skyrocket forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump well suited to shaded borders, rock gardens, and container plantings.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Pink Skyrocket is a distinctive foamflower cultivar with very narrow, deeply and sharply cut, almost spidery leaflets — among the most finely dissected foliage in the genus — giving the clump a delicate, lacy texture quite different from the broader, maple-like leaves of most Tiarella. In spring, slim spikes crowded with small, star-shaped, pink-flushed flowers rise just above the foliage, deepening the pink tones already present in the new leaves. The refined, textural foliage remains an asset through the whole season, long after bloom has finished, making this a strong choice for a woodland shade garden or as a textural accent among broader-leaved shade perennials like hostas and heucheras. Zone 4–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
